query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, low‐temperature annealing treatment that promotes selective interfacial segregation at the lamellar colony boundaries in the eutectic high‐entropy alloy can smooth the abrupt phase interfaces, enhance dislocation transmission, reduce local stress concentrations, and thereby overcome brittleness while retaining or improving tensile strength at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies having sharp, chemically and structurally abrupt internal boundaries that lead to dislocation pile-ups.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment designed to induce beneficial interfacial segregation/modification at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room‐temperature tensile deformation under standard mechanical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified interphase boundaries with tailored chemistry and a slightly softened gradient that mitigates abrupt mechanical mismatch.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced dislocation transmission across the formerly sharp interfaces reduces dislocation pile-up, local stress concentrations, and microcrack initiation, thereby increasing tensile ductility without compromising, and possibly enhancing, strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room‐temperature ductility (increased strain to failure) while maintaining or modestly increasing tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic HEA with dual‐phase lamellar colonies exhibiting sharp boundaries and limited tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated under ambient temperature tensile loading; the microstructural modifications must remain stable during service to preserve strength and ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in ductility and strength is uncertain and will depend on the precise annealing parameters and resulting interfacial chemistry. Further experimental validation is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples; treat one set with the controlled low‐temperature annealing to promote interface segregation, and leave the other as untreated controls. Subject both sets to room-temperature tensile tests and detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, SEM, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) to evaluate dislocation behavior near the lamellar boundaries.
measurements: Tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation to failure
Quantitative assessment of interfacial segregation and interface width
TEM observations of dislocation patterns and pile-ups at the boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in ductility (i.e., similar or lower elongation to failure) or if there is a reduction in tensile strength compared to the untreated alloy, or if TEM does not reveal reduced dislocation pile-up at the modified interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

frame.goal: Overcome room-temperature tensile brittleness by increasing ductility while retaining or boosting strength.

frame.understanding: The brittleness arises from the inability of the pre‐existing sharp internal boundaries within the lamellar colonies to effectively transmit dislocations, causing stress localization. By modifying these interfaces, dislocation transmission may be enhanced, thereby reducing stress concentrations and preventing premature crack initiation.

decision.trend: The early work on eutectic HEAs—in particular the 2014 study—focused on obtaining a dual‐phase lamellar microstructure via casting routes, which yielded high strength but suffered from brittle behavior at room temperature due to the abrupt, non‐accommodating internal interfaces. Later, multi‐step processing such as cold rolling or elaborate thermo-mechanical sequences were explored to tweak ductility, yet these efforts primarily modified the overall microstructure (e.g., refining features or introducing deformation-induced changes) without specifically addressing the discontinuous nature of the phase boundaries that cause dislocation pile-ups and localized stress concentrations.
decision.unsolved: The intrinsic inability of the sharp, coherent interfaces in the dual‐phase lamellar colonies to effectively transmit dislocations remains unresolved, leading to local stress buildup and premature cracking. Specifically, the challenge is to engineer the interphase boundaries such that they promote dislocation transfer, reduce stress concentrations, and thus overcome limited room-temperature ductility without sacrificing the existing strength.
decision.lever: Implement a targeted interface modification—such as a controlled low-temperature annealing or surface treatment that induces beneficial interfacial segregation—to tailor the chemistry and structure of the lamellar boundaries, thereby enhancing dislocation transmission
decision.why: This approach directly targets the root cause of the brittleness by softening the mismatch at the internal interfaces without altering the overall phase composition or microstructure architecture. It is a single intervention that builds on the prior trend by moving from bulk processing to precise, localized boundary engineering, enabling an improvement in ductility while retaining or possibly even boosting strength under room-temperature tensile conditions.
